The margin of error for a confidence interval is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size and directly proportional to the critical value associated with the confidence level. Increasing the sample size (Change 2) reduces the margin of error, yielding a narrower interval. Conversely, increasing the confidence level (Change 1) requires a larger critical value, which widens the interval. Standard introductory statistics logic dictates that to achieve a narrower interval, one should only implement the change that actively decreases the interval's width (Change 2) and avoid the change that increases it.

The 95% refers to the success rate of the estimation procedure over the long run, not the probability of a specific realized interval containing the mean.
Statement D is True: Because 95% confidence intervals are designed to capture the true population mean in 95% of repeated samples, constructing 200 independent intervals would lead us to expect roughly 95% of them (0.95 × 200 = 190) to contain the true mean.
